embedding_text:
Troubleshooting Streaks and Blotches on Canon PIXMA MG3620 Printers

## Safe troubleshooting steps

Start by confirming whether the issue appears on both plain-text pages and photo
prints. Ask the customer to print a nozzle check pattern and keep the page as
evidence. If gaps or smearing appear, the customer can run one standard head
cleaning, wait five minutes, and print a second nozzle check. If the pattern is
still poor, one deep cleaning cycle is acceptable. Support should not ask the
customer to repeat cleaning over and over, because excessive cleaning consumes
ink without resolving a hardware defect.

The customer may also confirm that the cartridges are seated correctly, remove
any protective tape that was left in place, and test with fresh paper stored in
a dry location. If borderless photo output is affected but text pages are
clean, support should ask for one standard document sample and one photo sample
before moving on.

Preparing Latency Evidence Before a Server Management Consultation

## What the customer provides

Ask the customer for the date and approximate time of at least three recent
latency events, which applications or services were affected, and whether the
slowdown was visible to end users or only to administrators. Helpful evidence
includes CPU, memory, disk, and network utilization from the same period;
server role labels; recent patching or deployment activity; and whether the
problem appeared on one system or across a cluster. A brief note about business
impact, such as delayed request handling or missed job windows, helps support
prioritize the consultation.

Customers should gather evidence only through existing dashboards, operating
system counters, or exported logs. They should not change live performance
settings, restart services, or disable protections solely to produce data.

Preparing Latency Evidence Before a Server Management Consultation

## What support provides

Support reviews the evidence package, highlights missing comparisons, and tells
the customer whether the first consultation should focus on workload patterns,
capacity management, or operational process. Support may ask for one additional
peak-time sample if the supplied metrics do not align with the reported slow
window. The specialist then uses the collected evidence to discuss best
practices for inspections, alerting coverage, and routine management.

Support should encourage the customer to compare one slow period with one normal
period whenever possible. That contrast often shows whether the issue is tied to
resource saturation, scheduled jobs, or an external dependency. If no baseline
exists, the customer can still capture future timestamps and exported counters;
they should not stress-test live systems merely to create a data sample for the
consultation.

Support reviews the intake information and prepares a discovery worksheet that
maps request sources, queue owners, priority rules, and handoff points. During
the consultation, support helps identify where delays occur, whether the
workflow needs additional statuses, and where a simpler intake form would
improve adoption. Recommendations may cover prioritization logic, queue design,
and change-approval flow, but only after the current process is understood.

If the customer highlights ease of use or customer-support integration, support
should ask for specific friction points such as duplicate entry, unclear queue
ownership, or delayed handoff between teams. Sample forms, one week of typical
requests, and a list of must-have reports are often enough to make the first
session concrete without pretending the workflow can be redesigned from a single
email.
